ROADS OF GOLD

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Public funds have been used to pay for G FIP- Gauteng's Freeway Improvement Plan, but what if I told you they spent 3 times more than they should have per road?

Unique Selling Point:
In 2007 The Gauteng Freeway Improvement Plan (known as “G FIP”) was approved – a plan to update or newly construct several roads in Gauteng. The plan was then tendered, and several roads were meant to be done in time for the 2010 world cup. Initial costs were estimated at 8 billion. And the majority of the completion dates were from early to mid 2009. http://www.nra.co.za/live/content.php?Session_ID=80cb5df55518542ed007349d67f9b05d&Item_ID=260
In 2008 there was a public outcry regarding the costs of the 2010 FIFA world cup stadiums, and this lead to there being an investigation into GFIP.
According to calculations done by an engineering contractor – SOURCE JONES with more than 48 years in the roads construction business, (the source is an industry professional in South Africa and the rest of Africa) - South African Tax Payers are paying 3 times the price for one of SANRAL’s roads than in anywhere else in Africa or the world. (We have comparisons of other African’s nations and other far more complicated projects in the world.) G FIPs roads are tolled and the project was to either build new roads, or update (repave/ widen) other roads – the amount km’s is in contention. 185km verse 201km both of which are in SANRALs own reports. Please see MAP that shows the intended areas. The various sections of the roads were split up into 15 different packages (like Ingula) and each package was given to a construction company. (2 more packages were later added but are also in contention as SANRAL has also not been forthcoming regarding their tender bid documents etc)
In 2011, the competition commission reported that 15 companies were actually working together to up the prices and charge more – these consortiums were fined individually (each split up- and we have that report it totalled 1.4 billion rand in fines) depending on how guilty they were found of “unfair practices”. The following companies are the ones we will focus on, and these were their fines”
Aveng: R306 million
Basil read: R95 million
Murray & Roberts: R309 million (A, B, E)
Raubex:R59 million (reported to be the whistleblower company – were not named but given a fine – possibly look for that whistleblower.)
WBHO: R311 million (package A, B, E)

BUT THE BIG QUESTION HAS ALWAYS BEEN: HOW MUCH HAVE WE OVERSPENT? WELL THE ENGINEER HAS PAINSTAKENLY WORKED THAT OUT!

We will take Nine of the 15 packages (the ones that had clear cut documents) : Total cost was R9.2 billion. The engineer found that R5.9 billion of that was actually “unfair value” meaning we should only have paid R3.3 billion.
Package F was marked for concern as the value of the steel used for reinforcing was in excess of R679 million!!!
SANRAL have said that only R700 million rand (tribunal only found R100 million was from collusion) of the project was collusion, but the engineer can prove that the number is closer R5.9 billion based on their own numbers.
In excel spreadsheets, again extrapolated from SANRAL’s own documents were have spent 18 billion on this, and it was budgeted as only R8 billion. Where has the 10 billion gone?


Summary:
We will focus on several of these companies and will again prove that they have charged us 3 times the price of any other road – some prices were upped by +400% per km. Package F (Buccleuch to Gillooly’s) had a price in excess of R74 million per kilometre, some other packages in excess of 140 million per km. (The reasonable cost should be no more than R29 million per kilometre.)
All cost estimates were taken from SANRAL’s own slide documents, and the engineer was prudent and based his estimates on industry standard rates (SANRAL’ s own bill of quantities) and added more than 15% contingency – in fact, the source added 25%! And then still added the Contractors Ps & Gs – costs and profit margins.
By 2013, all the contractors were found guilty of corruption in this regard with corrupt tender processes. The hearings were conducted by the Competition Tribunal in July 2013. The report from the CIDB was made public in September 2013.


Further information:
I am meeting with sources on Monday. The story would air on the Sunday 30 October 2016. It's exclusive and OUTA would hold a press conference the Monday after.

Press Release:


Gauteng Freeways
In 2013 the Competition Commission found contractors guilty of collusion during construction of Gauteng’s new tolled freeways. This tender bid rigging process resulted in the province’s freeways costing taxpayers several billion rand more than anticipated. Carte Blanche tallies the cost of the Gauteng Freeway Improvement Project.
Producer: Sasha Schwendenwein
Presenter: Devi Sankaree Govender
Researcher: Laura Byrne


Script:


Back in 2005 Gauteng’s highways were a congested nightmare. The South African National Roads Agency or SANRAL’s solution came in the form of the Gauteng Freeway Improvement Project, known as GFIP. Today, only some of Gauteng’s drivers are, somewhat reluctantly, paying for this project through the highly contentious etolling system.
Voxpop 1: “I don’t have an eTag because it’s too expensive for me.”
Voxpop 2: “It’s affecting the economy negatively.”
Voxpop 3: “The rich are always benefitting, and now, us, the poor, we have to pay for that.”
GRAPHIC: So, what are we paying for? Construction on the GFIP began in 2007. Generally, the upgrades included the addition of new concrete barriers and lighting. The roads were all widened, most by 1- 2 lanes. All the updated roads were repaved with new bitumen rubber asphalt, and repainted.
34 interchanges were upgraded and 47 new bridges and 4 new directional ramps added.
INITIALLY ESTIMATED AT R4.6 BILLION, GFIP BALLOONED TO R17.9 BILLION. AND SOME EXPERTS ARE SAYING WE’VE PAID AN ASTONISHING R96MN PER KILOMETRE OF HIGHWAY. CIVIL SOCIETY IS NOT GOING TO LET THAT GO.
Wayne: “We have been ripped off, you and I, the public in this country by around 10 billion rand and that is the sin.”
Wayne Duvenage chairman of the civil action group OUTA explains that in order to repay the costs of the GFIP, the roads agency earmarked 201km of Gauteng’s highways for the controversial e-tolling system .
Wayne: “The fees are more than double what they should be.”
In late January SANRAL sent out 8000 summonses to users for their unpaid etoll bills.
Wayne: “The tolling matter is collapsing, it’s failed, its less than 20% compliance now, so 80% of people aren’t paying.”
The roads agency are in financial trouble and many have criticised the high costs of the collection process alone.
Wayne: “So the etoll costs over a billion rand a year, just to administer, before one rand goes into the tarmac.”
Dave: “You are totally convinced you are being ripped off.”
Dave Zietsman is a 46 year veteran road surveyor and civil engineer.
Dave: “One minute you have our politicians so enthusiastic about being anti e-tolls then all of a sudden after 2014 the elections, they all just seemed to have fizzled into nothing.”
Dave asked how the improved freeway could have cost on average 96 million rand per kilometre (17.9 / 185km)? That’s almost as much as the Gautrain at 100 mill/km, but that involved major underground excavation.
LINK: THE GFIP WAS ONE OF SEVERAL MAJOR CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS IN PREPARATION FOR THE 2010 SOCCER WORLD CUP. FEW WOULD SUSPECT THAT THE COMPETITION COMMISSION TRIBUNAL WOULD FIND SOME OF CONTRACTORS GUILTY OF COLLUSION WHICH WOULD ULTIMATELY HAVE AN IMPACT ON TAXPAYER’S POCKETS AND THE COST OF ETOLLS.
The person responsible for the commission’s investigation is Makgale Mohlala (Magg-al-e Mog-la-la) the cartel’s division manager.
Makgale: “Collusion, is on their very nature designed to inflate prices, the ultimate aim is to make super profits.”
Link: GFIP WAS BROKEN DOWN INTO SEVERAL SECTIONS, CALLED PACKAGES. THE COMPETITION COMMISSION FOUND COLLUSION DID OCCUR WITH PACKAGE A, PACKAGE B AND PACKAGES E1+ E2.
Using several SANRAL presentations Dave estimated how much these packages should have cost.
Dave: “I didn’t work from a bill of quantities that I invented. The engineers gave precise quantities for major items of work.”
He generously added a 25% contingency fee and 10% for inflation. He also used higher 2012 prices for a 2008 construction project.
According to Dave: Package A, should have cost R44 million per kilometre. SANRAL spent R79 million.
Package B, should have cost R39 million per kilometre. SANRAL spent R104 million.
And, packages E1 and 2, should have cost R70 million per kilometre. SANRAL spent R151 million.
LINK: THE COMPETITION COMMISSION BELIEVED THERE WAS A CASE TO ANSWER FOR.
Makgale: “The first firm that approached the commission disclosed that collusion in the construction sector is a way of doing business.”
Makgale explains that when the commission announced they were investigating the construction cartels, the firms raced to disclose the collusion details in exchange for corporate leniency.
Makgale: “Corporate leniency is a policy in which the commission is able to grant a firm, that comes first, immunity from prosecution.”
Makgale says firm Group 5 disclosed that they had colluded with 3 other firms on the GFIP in exchange for immunity. Group 5 implicated Concor, a subsidiary of Murray and Roberts, Stefanutti Stocks and Wilson Bayly Holmes Ovcon, known as WBHO.
Makgale: “They agreed to share the packages among themselves and then in order to ensure that the arrangement works well, they are going to exchange cover prices, I tell you my price. So that you know you have to price above me if the project is designated to be won by myself.”
In a written response to Carte Blanche, Group 5 denies any involvement in the collusive deal. Makgale says Group 5 ultimately pulled out of the collusion agreement and entered lower cover prices than the other firms.
Makgale: “Group 5 pulled out, so they didn’t honour their arrangement and they won all the packages.”
Makgale says Group 5 didn’t have the capacity to fulfil all 3 packages and SANRAL awarded package B to WBHO.
Group 5 says they won the packages by submitting the lowest most competitive prices. WBHO and GROUP 5 both said the costs of the packages were understandable and fair. Concor declined to comment as they didn’t win or deliver any projects for GFIP.
Peter: “This was foreign to me, any collusion, this was just wrong.”
Retired road contractor and civil engineer Peter Brauteseth (Braut-e-seth) has spent a lifetime building roads. He explains how contractors generally collude.
Peter: “This job’s worth a hundred million. There are 5 jobs. You’re going to get job 1, you’re going to get job 2. And what we’ll do, we’ll put 20 million on this 100 million. And the guys that back off will each get five million.
LINK: THE QUESTION IS, NOW THAT COLLUSION HAS BEEN PROVEN WHAT SHOULD WE HAVE PAID FOR THE GAUTENG FREEWAY IMPROVEMENT PROJECT?
Wayne: “SANRAL tells us, that their sums, and that that collusion practice was only responsible for about R750 million, and in fact they say, not all of it was from the GFIP.”
LINK: SANRAL POO’POO’D OUTA’S INITIAL REPORT LAST YEAR FOR LACK OF RESEARCH. AND SO OUTA REQUESTED THE TENDER DOCUMENTS FOR GFIP AS SANRAL HAD NEVER MADE THEM PUBLIC. THAT WAS 6 MONTHS AGO. THEN, IN NOVEMBER LAST YEAR, CARTE BLANCHE ALSO REQUESTED THE SAME INFORMATION.
Wayne: “SANRAL, if you’re still trying to defend this position, that 17 billion rand is fair price for that road upgrade, we’re saying wrong.”
Dave’s initial calculations were based on SANRAL’s estimates, but SANRAL could argue that Dave’s findings were wrong because they aren’t based on actual tender documents.
LINK: THEN, PETER GOT HIS HANDS ON THE VERY TENDER DOCUMENTS - FOR PACKAGE G.
Peter: “It was R190 million off the tendered price. I think section G was 17km, so I work it out. R10 million a kilometre too much.”
Wayne: “We believe that SANRAL could have built 3 Gauteng freeway improvement projects.”
OUTA set up a unit specifically to investigate the GFIP cost conundrum anew and requested SANRAL’s input.
Wayne: “It wasn’t a full new road build project it was a rehabilitation, resurfacing and 27% was new.”
OUTA used 3 different methods to cost the GFIP project.
Wayne: “We’ve gone deeper now to make sure that we have corroborated our facts with engineers input, quantity surveyors input.”
First, OUTA applied Dave and Peter’s calculations to the packages, THEN THEY analysed satellite imagery to work out the road surface area per meter, and FINALLY THEY made benchmark comparisons with other projects in South Africa, Africa and the World.
Wayne: “The Gauteng freeway improvement program should not have cost anything more than around 8 billion rand. It cost SANRAL R18 billion.”
WBHO say the calculations look like guesswork and are highly speculative and must be disregarded, as they were not based on the exact tenders bill of Quantities.
The competition commission fined Fifteen firms collectively R1.5 billion. Concor, Stefanutti Stocks and WBHO were fined for the collusive meeting on GFIP, amongst other projects. In their written response to Carte Blanche Stefanutti indicated that the employees who engaged in the tender process no longer work for them.
WBHO’s written feedback said they regret their conduct, but the tribunals findings ‘represented less than 1% of their 4000 tender bids since 2004. They believed the fine was excessive. GROUP 5 said they were not fined for any collusive arrangement on the GFIP project.
Makgale: “We’ve been able to actually sow a mistrust among them, so they can’t really be thinking of trusting each other after everything.”
LINK: THREE YEARS AFTER THE COMPETITION COMMISSION’S FINDINGS IN MAY 2016, SANRAL INSTITUTED CIVIL CLAIMS AGAINST 7 OF THE CONTRACTORS.
Wayne: “We believe that sanral are party to the problem here, and if they couldn’t pick up this overpricing, we’ve got to get to the bottom of that.”
But then in October 2016, Government settled all civil claims on behalf of SANRAL by making a deal with 7 of the contractors who admitted to the tribunal that they had engaged in uncompetitive practices on projects including GFIP.
Makgale: “Firms that are facing charges before the tribunal, those charges are proceeding.”
The firms agreed to collectively pay another R1.5 billion over 12 years into a “socio-economic development fund.” But, critics of this deal say the money should have gone back into the fiscus.
Wayne: “Government should have gone after the collusive companies to claw back all of the overcharges.”
All 4 companies declined on-camera interviews, but Group 5 said the agreement made with government is groundbreaking.
LINK: WE ASKED SANRAL FOR AN INTERVIEW LAST YEAR AND AGAIN THIS YEAR. THEY DECLINED CITING THE AGREEMENT THEY MADE WITH THE CONTRACTORS LAST YEAR.
We wrote further questions to SANRAL, and Vusi Mona the General Manager of Communications responded to say, they would make the tender documents available to OUTA, that SANRAL had nothing to add to the matters raised in our questions and that as a state-owned entity they would abide by the settlement agreement.
Wayne: “We believe the minister needs to call for a commission of enquiry or an independent enquiry and look at this because this is serious.”

Makgale: “Group 5 pulled out, so they didn’t honour their arrangement and they won all the packages.” Makgale says Group 5 didn’t have the capacity to fulfil all 3 packages and SANRAL awarded package B to WBHO. Group 5 says they won the packages by submitting the lowest most competitive prices. WBHO and GROUP 5 both said the costs of the packages were understandable and fair. Concor declined to comment as they didn’t win or deliver any projects for GFIP. Peter: “This was foreign to me, any collusion, this was just wrong.” Retired road contractor and civil engineer Peter Brauteseth (Braut-e-seth) has spent a lifetime building roads. He explains how contractors generally collude. Peter: “This job’s worth a hundred million. There are 5 jobs. You’re going to get job 1, you’re going to get job 2. And what we’ll do, we’ll put 20 million on this 100 million. And the guys that back off will each get five million. LINK: THE QUESTION IS, NOW THAT COLLUSION HAS BEEN PROVEN WHAT SHOULD WE HAVE PAID FOR THE GAUTENG FREEWAY IMPROVEMENT PROJECT? Wayne: “SANRAL tells us, that their sums, and that that collusion practice was only responsible for about R750 million, and in fact they say, not all of it was from the GFIP.” LINK: SANRAL POO’POO’D OUTA’S INITIAL REPORT LAST YEAR FOR LACK OF RESEARCH. AND SO OUTA REQUESTED THE TENDER DOCUMENTS FOR GFIP AS SANRAL HAD NEVER MADE THEM PUBLIC. THAT WAS 6 MONTHS AGO. THEN, IN NOVEMBER LAST YEAR, CARTE BLANCHE ALSO REQUESTED THE SAME INFORMATION. Wayne: “SANRAL, if you’re still trying to defend this position, that 17 billion rand is fair price for that road upgrade, we’re saying wrong.” Dave’s initial calculations were based on SANRAL’s estimates, but SANRAL could argue that Dave’s findings were wrong because they aren’t based on actual tender documents. LINK: THEN, PETER GOT HIS HANDS ON THE VERY TENDER DOCUMENTS - FOR PACKAGE G. Peter: “It was R190 million off the tendered price. I think section G was 17km, so I work it out. R10 million a kilometre too much.” Wayne: “We believe that SANRAL could have built 3 Gauteng freeway improvement projects.” OUTA set up a unit specifically to investigate the GFIP cost conundrum anew and requested SANRAL’s input. Wayne: “It wasn’t a full new road build project it was a rehabilitation, resurfacing and 27% was new.” OUTA used 3 different methods to cost the GFIP project. Wayne: “We’ve gone deeper now to make sure that we have corroborated our facts with engineers input, quantity surveyors input.” First, OUTA applied Dave and Peter’s calculations to the packages, THEN THEY analysed satellite imagery to work out the road surface area per meter, and FINALLY THEY made benchmark comparisons with other projects in South Africa, Africa and the World. Wayne: “The Gauteng freeway improvement program should not have cost anything more than around 8 billion rand. It cost SANRAL R18 billion.” WBHO say the calculations look like guesswork and are highly speculative and must be disregarded, as they were not based on the exact tenders bill of Quantities. The competition commission fined Fifteen firms collectively R1.5 billion. Concor, Stefanutti Stocks and WBHO were fined for the collusive meeting on GFIP, amongst other projects. In their written response to Carte Blanche Stefanutti indicated that the employees who engaged in the tender process no longer work for them. WBHO’s written feedback said they regret their conduct, but the tribunals findings ‘represented less than 1% of their 4000 tender bids since 2004. They believed the fine was excessive. GROUP 5 said they were not fined for any collusive arrangement on the GFIP project. Makgale: “We’ve been able to actually sow a mistrust among them, so they can’t really be thinking of trusting each other after everything.” LINK: THREE YEARS AFTER THE COMPETITION COMMISSION’S FINDINGS IN MAY 2016, SANRAL INSTITUTED CIVIL CLAIMS AGAINST 7 OF THE CONTRACTORS. Wayne: “We believe that sanral are party to the problem here, and if they couldn’t pick up this overpricing, we’ve got to get to the bottom of that.” But then in October 2016, Government settled all civil claims on behalf of SANRAL by making a deal with 7 of the contractors who admitted to the tribunal that they had engaged in uncompetitive practices on projects including GFIP. Makgale: “Firms that are facing charges before the tribunal, those charges are proceeding.” The firms agreed to collectively pay another R1.5 billion over 12 years into a “socio-economic development fund.” But, critics of this deal say the money should have gone back into the fiscus. Wayne: “Government should have gone after the collusive companies to claw back all of the overcharges.” All 4 companies declined on-camera interviews, but Group 5 said the agreement made with government is groundbreaking. LINK: WE ASKED SANRAL FOR AN INTERVIEW LAST YEAR AND AGAIN THIS YEAR. THEY DECLINED CITING THE AGREEMENT THEY MADE WITH THE CONTRACTORS LAST YEAR. We wrote further questions to SANRAL, and Vusi Mona the General Manager of Communications responded to say, they would make the tender documents available to OUTA, that SANRAL had nothing to add to the matters raised in our questions and that as a state-owned entity they would abide by the settlement agreement. Wayne: “We believe the minister needs to call for a commission of enquiry or an independent enquiry and look at this because this is serious.”

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Public funds have been used to pay for G FIP- Gauteng's Freeway Improvement Plan, but what if I told you they spent 3 times more than they should have per road?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In 2007 The Gauteng Freeway Improvement Plan (known as “G FIP”) was approved – a plan to update or newly construct several roads in Gauteng. The plan was then tendered, and several roads were meant to be done in time for the 2010 world cup. Initial costs were estimated at 8 billion. And the majority of the completion dates were from early to mid 2009. http://www.nra.co.za/live/content.php?Session_ID=80cb5df55518542ed007349d67f9b05d&Item_ID=260 In 2008 there was a public outcry regarding the costs of the 2010 FIFA world cup stadiums, and this lead to there being an investigation into GFIP. According to calculations done by an engineering contractor – SOURCE JONES with more than 48 years in the roads construction business, (the source is an industry professional in South Africa and the rest of Africa) - South African Tax Payers are paying 3 times the price for one of SANRAL’s roads than in anywhere else in Africa or the world. (We have comparisons of other African’s nations and other far more complicated projects in the world.) G FIPs roads are tolled and the project was to either build new roads, or update (repave/ widen) other roads – the amount km’s is in contention. 185km verse 201km both of which are in SANRALs own reports. Please see MAP that shows the intended areas. The various sections of the roads were split up into 15 different packages (like Ingula) and each package was given to a construction company. (2 more packages were later added but are also in contention as SANRAL has also not been forthcoming regarding their tender bid documents etc) In 2011, the competition commission reported that 15 companies were actually working together to up the prices and charge more – these consortiums were fined individually (each split up- and we have that report it totalled 1.4 billion rand in fines) depending on how guilty they were found of “unfair practices”. The following companies are the ones we will focus on, and these were their fines” Aveng: R306 million Basil read: R95 million Murray & Roberts: R309 million (A, B, E) Raubex:R59 million (reported to be the whistleblower company – were not named but given a fine – possibly look for that whistleblower.) WBHO: R311 million (package A, B, E) BUT THE BIG QUESTION HAS ALWAYS BEEN: HOW MUCH HAVE WE OVERSPENT? WELL THE ENGINEER HAS PAINSTAKENLY WORKED THAT OUT! We will take Nine of the 15 packages (the ones that had clear cut documents) : Total cost was R9.2 billion. The engineer found that R5.9 billion of that was actually “unfair value” meaning we should only have paid R3.3 billion. Package F was marked for concern as the value of the steel used for reinforcing was in excess of R679 million!!! SANRAL have said that only R700 million rand (tribunal only found R100 million was from collusion) of the project was collusion, but the engineer can prove that the number is closer R5.9 billion based on their own numbers. In excel spreadsheets, again extrapolated from SANRAL’s own documents were have spent 18 billion on this, and it was budgeted as only R8 billion. Where has the 10 billion gone?
metadata.Summary: We will focus on several of these companies and will again prove that they have charged us 3 times the price of any other road – some prices were upped by +400% per km. Package F (Buccleuch to Gillooly’s) had a price in excess of R74 million per kilometre, some other packages in excess of 140 million per km. (The reasonable cost should be no more than R29 million per kilometre.) All cost estimates were taken from SANRAL’s own slide documents, and the engineer was prudent and based his estimates on industry standard rates (SANRAL’ s own bill of quantities) and added more than 15% contingency – in fact, the source added 25%! And then still added the Contractors Ps & Gs – costs and profit margins. By 2013, all the contractors were found guilty of corruption in this regard with corrupt tender processes. The hearings were conducted by the Competition Tribunal in July 2013. The report from the CIDB was made public in September 2013.
